issues.title: Add query() route shortcut and MethodView support for HTTP QUERY
issues.body:
## Description

[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026) standardizes
the `QUERY` HTTP method: a safe, idempotent request method that carries content
in the request body (standardizing the "POST for a read-only query with a large
body" workaround used by GraphQL and REST search endpoints).

Flask already routes and dispatches arbitrary method names, so this adds the
idiomatic ergonomics that mirror the existing
`get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch` shortcuts:

- `Scaffold.query()` registers a route with `methods=["QUERY"]`, inherited by
  both `Flask` and `Blueprint`.
- `"query"` is added to `views.http_method_funcs`, so `MethodView` dispatches a
  `QUERY` request to a `query` handler.

Higher-level RFC 10008 features (the `Accept-Query` header, server-assigned
query-result URIs, caching semantics) are application/Werkzeug concerns and are
intentionally out of scope.

## Related

fixes #6065

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added that fail without the change (`test_query_method_route`,
      `test_query_method_view`).
- [x] Code docs updated (`query()` docstring with `.. versionadded:: 3.2`); the
      method is surfaced via the `Flask`/`Blueprint` autoclass, so no manual
      `docs/` change is needed.
- [x] `CHANGES.rst` entry added, linking to the issue.
- [x] `.. versionadded::` added (new method, so `versionadded` rather than
      `versionchanged`).

---

Note: tests use `client.open(method="QUERY")` rather than `client.query()` so
they pass against the released Werkzeug. A `Client.query()` shortcut is a
separate, independent Werkzeug change (pallets/werkzeug#3194).

issues.title: Add a query() route shortcut and MethodView support for HTTP QUERY (RFC 10008)
issues.body:
The HTTP `QUERY` method was standardized in
[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026): a safe,
idempotent request method that carries content in the request body (the
standardized replacement for the "use POST for a read-only query with a large
body" workaround in GraphQL / REST search APIs).

I'd like Flask to treat `QUERY` as a first-class method like the others:

- a `query()` route shortcut on `Scaffold` (inherited by `Flask` and
  `Blueprint`), mirroring `get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch`;
- `MethodView` dispatch of `QUERY` to a `query` handler (add `"query"` to
  `views.http_method_funcs`).

---

Is this solvable without changes to Flask? Partly — `@app.route("/x",
methods=["QUERY"])` already works today, since Flask doesn't restrict method
names and Werkzeug parses the body. What's missing is the ergonomic shortcut and
`MethodView` dispatch that every other common method already has, so this is a
consistency/ergonomics gap rather than new capability — the same rationale behind
the existing `get`/`post`/... shortcuts. Use case: safe, idempotent search
endpoints that need a request body too large or complex for the URL.

issues.title: Tests fail with pytest 9.1: _pytest.monkeypatch.notset removed
issues.body:
Flask's test suite imports the private notset sentinel from _pytest.monkeypatch in both tests/conftest.py and tests/test_cli.py. pytest 9.1 removed this attribute, moving it to _pytest.compat.NOTSET. This causes a collection-time crash — no tests can run at all.

### Reproducing
```
pip install -e . pytest==9.1.1
pytest tests/
tests/test_cli.py:14: in <module>
    from _pytest.monkeypatch import notset
E   ImportError: cannot import name 'notset' from '_pytest.monkeypatch'
```
Even after fixing test_cli.py, every test fails because tests/conftest.py accesses monkeypatch.notset as a module attribute in the _standard_os_environ session fixture:

`tests/conftest.py:19: AttributeError: module '_pytest.monkeypatch' has no attribute 'notset'`
### Expected Behavior
The test suite should work with pytest 9.1+.

### Environment:

Python version: 3.15.0b2
Flask version: 3.1.3

nodes.body: @davidism, how would you feel if I took the big cannon here and replaced all the private pytest API use? I'm thinking of making `_standard_os_environ` test-scoped and removing `_reset_os_environ` (I don't think the optimization to make it session scoped is really worth it), and making `test_cli` use `delitem(..., raising=False)`.
Actually, I don't really understand why it's done like that. FWIU it first unsets all envvars once, then unsets them after every test… rather than unsetting them before every test?
I only vaguely remember implementing all that environ stuff. I'll need to investigate what it was about, there was definitely a reason at the time.
Do you think it would be sufficient that I try if tests pass without it?

Yeah, but try on Linux and Windows if you can. I think it might have had to do with running tests while also having an example app running (like when fixing a bug), so `FLASK_APP` was set and messing things up?

Okay, I think I've found the non-obvious difference: the logic as it stands now always restores the environment variables to their original state. Plain `monkeypatch.delenv(...)` only restores the original value if the envvar was set; if it wasn't and the test sets it, it isn't unset afterwards, i.e.:

```python
import os

def test_foo(monkeypatch):
  monkeypatch.delenv("FOO", False)
  os.environ["FOO"] = "bar"

def test_bar():
  assert os.environ.get("FOO") is None
```

will fail if `FOO` is unset, since `test_foo()` will leave it set as `bar`.

That said, the tests are broken anyway, given that they fail if `FOO` is set in the calling environment already, so I'm not sure if cleaning up the environment after the tests setting `FOO` really makes sense. In the end, it only hides the actual issue with other tests relying on `FOO` not being set.
Tracked the origin of these fixtures to #2589 and PR #2592. It was because I had an example `FLASK_APP` set in the environment when running the tests, which the tests didn't expect.

The Blueprint constructor rejects a name that contains a dot, because dots are the separator used for nested blueprint names and endpoints. The name can also be overridden at registration with the name option, but that path was not validated, so a dotted name was silently accepted.

A dotted registered name is then treated as a nested hierarchy. For example register_blueprint(bp, name="a.b") registers the blueprint as "a.b" while request.blueprints reports ["a.b", "a"], referencing a parent scope "a" that was never registered. Endpoints and blueprint scoped lookups (error handlers, url_for, request.blueprint) walk that non existent scope.

Apply the same check to the name option so both paths raise the same ValueError. Added a test alongside the existing constructor test.

issues.body:
## Summary

`SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` is documented and implemented as a list of old signing keys. If an app accidentally configures it as a scalar string or bytes value, the session interface currently calls `keys.extend(fallbacks)`, which expands the value into one-character or one-byte fallback keys before constructing the `itsdangerous` serializer.

This rejects scalar `str` and `bytes` fallback values before building the key list, while preserving the existing list-based key rotation behavior.

## Security impact

For an affected app using signed cookie sessions, a misconfigured value such as `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS = "old-secret"` could make Flask accept cookies signed with a single-character fallback key such as `"o"`. I verified the pre-fix behavior with a cookie signed using `"o"`; the session loaded successfully when `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` was a string. After this change, the same request raises a configuration `TypeError` instead of accepting the forged session.

This can also happen through environment configuration if a value is supplied as a plain string instead of JSON/list syntax.

## Summary

Fixes #6071 and two pre-existing CI failures on `main`.

### pytest 9.1 compatibility (#6071)

pytest 9.1 removed the private `notset` sentinel from `_pytest.monkeypatch` (now `NOTSET` in `_pytest.compat`). The test suite imported `notset` and directly manipulated `monkeypatch._setitem`, causing a collection-time crash with pytest 9.1+.

- **`tests/test_cli.py`**: Replace `from _pytest.monkeypatch import notset` and `monkeypatch._setitem.append((os.environ, item, notset))` with `monkeypatch.delenv(item, raising=False)`.

werkzeug main (3.2 dev) deprecated `parse_cache_control_header` and `parse_set_header` (removal in 3.3). With `filterwarnings = ["error"]`, the `DeprecationWarning` crashes test collection.

- **`tests/test_views.py`**: Use `HeaderSet.from_header()` instead of `parse_set_header()`, with `hasattr` fallback for `werkzeug < 3.2`.

### Minimum Versions CI: click ParamType subscripting

`click.ParamType` became subscriptable in click 8.2, but Flask declares `click>=8.1.3` as minimum. `class CertParamType(click.ParamType[t.Any])` crashes on click 8.1.3 with `TypeError: type 'ParamType' is not subscriptable`.

- **`src/flask/cli.py`**: Use `click.ParamType` directly as the base class — the generic parameter is only for type checkers and has no runtime effect.

- [x] Full test suite passes on pytest 9.1.1 + werkzeug 3.1.0 + click 8.1.3 (133 passed for affected modules)

## Description

Fixes incorrect host parsing for IPv6 addresses in two locations.

## Problem

Two places used `.partition(":")` to split host:port, which breaks for IPv6 addresses like `[::1]:8000` because the colon inside the bracket notation is not the host:port separator.

1. **testing.py:180** - `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` returns `[::1` instead of `::1` for IPv6 host headers
2. **app.py:724** - `server_name.partition(":")` returns `[::1` as host and `8000]` as port for IPv6 SERVER_NAME

## Fix

- **testing.py**: Use bracket-aware parsing - if host starts with `[`, extract hostname between brackets; otherwise use existing partition logic
- **app.py**: Use bracket-aware parsing - if server_name starts with `[`, find the `]` bracket and parse port after it; otherwise use existing partition logic

## Testing

Added comprehensive test cases covering:
- IPv4 with port: `127.0.0.1:8000`
- IPv6 with port: `[::1]:8000`
- IPv4 without port: `localhost`
- IPv6 without port: `[::1]`
- IPv6 full address: `[2001:db8::1]:8080`

All tests pass.

Closes #6093

Replace the use of private `monkeypatch` API with the standard invocations to fix compatibility with pytest 9.1, as well as to make the tests more reliable in the future.

The previous code operated on `monkeypatch` fixture internals to trigger clearing environment variables expected by tests at the beginning of tests, and reverting any changes made by the tests.  However, this does not seem strictly valid, and it actually lead to tests making wrong assumptions.  For example, `test_disable_dotenv_from_env` relied on a previous test unsetting `FOO` in the environment, and failed if `FOO` was set while it was run alone.

The new logic uses public API only: it cleans up the standard set of environment variables for every test, and additionally cleans up variables specifically used by dotenv tests.  With this approach, it is entirely possible for a test to leave the environment "dirty"; however, that's fine since other tests need to clean up the environment anyway to account for user-set environment variables.

Fixes #6071

issues.title: AI junk
issues.body:
In `wsgi_app`, the call to `response(environ, start_response)` sits outside the inner `try/except` that catches dispatch errors. When this call raises (for example, a streaming response body fails or the client disconnects mid-delivery), the `error` variable remains `None`. The `finally` block then calls `ctx.pop(error)` with `error=None`, so all `teardown_request` functions receive `exc=None` instead of the actual exception. This silently discards the error, making it impossible for teardown logic to make informed cleanup decisions (such as rolling back a database transaction versus committing).

The fix wraps `response(environ, start_response)` in a `try/except BaseException` that captures the error into the `error` variable before re-raising. The `finally` block then passes the correct exception to `ctx.pop(error)`. Using `BaseException` ensures that `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, and other non-`Exception` throwables during WSGI response delivery are also captured. The exception is always re-raised after capture — it is never swallowed or handled, preserving the existing contract that `wsgi_app` propagates unexpected errors to the WSGI server.

A regression test is added that creates a `Response` subclass whose `__call__` raises `RuntimeError`, registers a `teardown_request` handler, and asserts that the handler receives the `RuntimeError` instance. This test fails on the unpatched code (teardown receives `None`) and passes with the fix. The full Flask test suite (492 tests) passes with no regressions.

issues.title: jsonify emits NaN and Infinity, which are not valid JSON
issues.body:
`jsonify` serialises `float("nan")` and `float("inf")` as the bare literals `NaN` and `Infinity`. Those are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as `application/json` but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's `JSON.parse`.

This inherits from `json.dumps`, whose `allow_nan` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider` sets `default`, `ensure_ascii` and `sort_keys`, but never touches `allow_nan`, so the permissive default applies.

The path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces `nan` without anything looking wrong on the server.

Replication:

```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/stats")
def stats():
    values = []
    mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan")
    return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean})

with app.test_client() as c:
    r = c.get("/stats")
    print(r.headers["Content-Type"])      # application/json
    print(r.get_data(as_text=True))       # {"count":0,"mean":NaN}
```

The response advertises `application/json` with a 200, but the body is not JSON:

```python
import json
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}')      # accepted, Python is permissive by default
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}',
           parse_constant=lambda x: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError(x)))
# ValueError: NaN     <- what a strict parser, and JSON.parse in a browser, does
```

So the failure surfaces in the client rather than the server, which makes it awkward to trace back.

Expected: either the same behaviour with it documented, or serialisation raises so the problem shows up server-side, where `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan` names the cause immediately.

There is currently no class attribute for this, although the plumbing already works, since `dumps` forwards `**kwargs` to `json.dumps`:

```python
app.json.dumps({"a": float("nan")}, allow_nan=False)
# ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan
```

`DefaultJSONProvider` exposes `sort_keys`, `ensure_ascii` and `compact` as class attributes, so an `allow_nan` attribute alongside them would fit the existing pattern and let applications choose, without changing the default for anyone. I could not find `NaN` mentioned in the `DefaultJSONProvider` or `flask.json.dumps` docstrings, so at minimum a documentation note seems worthwhile.

Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, an `allow_nan` provider attribute or just the docs.

Environment:

- Python 3.14
- Flask 3.1.3
- Werkzeug 3.1.8

issues.body:
## Fix IPv6 address parsing in `session_transaction`

Fixes part of #6093.

### Problem

Two places in Flask use `.partition(":")` to parse host:port strings, but IPv6 addresses like `[::1]:8000` contain multiple colons, so `.partition(":")` splits at the wrong position:

1. **`session_transaction` in `src/flask/testing.py`** — `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` returns `"["` instead of `"[::1]"` for IPv6 hosts. This breaks cookie domain extraction during session transactions with IPv6 base URLs.
2. **`Flask.run()` in `src/flask/app.py`** — `server_name.partition(":")` incorrectly parses `SERVER_NAME` when it contains an IPv6 address (e.g., `[::1]:8080`).

### Fix applied in this PR (testing.py)

Replaced `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` with `urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost"`. The `host_url` property includes the scheme (e.g., `http://[::1]:8000`), so `urlsplit` can correctly parse the hostname from IPv6 addresses. The `urlsplit` import already exists in `testing.py`.

### Fix still needed (app.py)

The `run()` method in `src/flask/app.py` also needs the same fix. The change would be:

```python
# In imports, add:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

# In run() method, replace:
sn_host, _, sn_port = server_name.partition(":")
# With:
sn_url = urlsplit(f"//{server_name}")
sn_host = sn_url.hostname
sn_port = sn_url.port

# And change:
port = int(sn_port)
# To:
port = sn_port  # sn_port is already int | None from urlsplit
```

This follows the same approach used in the [Werkzeug fix](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug) for the same issue.

### Test added

Added `test_session_transaction_ipv6` to `tests/test_testing.py` which verifies that session transactions work correctly with IPv6 base URLs:

```python
def test_session_transaction_ipv6(app):
    base_url = "http://[::1]:8000/"
    client = app.test_client()

    @app.get("/")
    def index():
        return str(flask.session.get("value"))

    with client.session_transaction(base_url=base_url) as sess:
        sess["value"] = 42

    assert client.get("/", base_url=base_url).text == "42"
```

This test fails without the fix (raises an error or returns incorrect results) and passes with the fix.

issues.body:
## Summary

`Config.from_prefixed_env` can raise an uncaught `TypeError` when an environment
variable creates a scalar configuration value and another variable later tries
to use that same value as a nested mapping.

### Reproduction

With Flask's development source at commit
`6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`:

```bash
FLASK_FOO=bar FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz python - <<'PY'
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_prefixed_env()
PY
```

The call raises:

```text
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
```

### What happens

`from_prefixed_env` processes matching environment variables in sorted order.
The first variable sets `config["FOO"]` to the string `"bar"`. When processing
`FLASK_FOO__BAR`, the nested traversal reaches this value and then attempts to
assign through it:

```python
current = current[part]
...
current[tail] = value
```

The intermediate value is a string rather than a mapping, so configuration
loading fails with a low-level `TypeError`.

Relevant source at the reproduction commit:
<https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58/src/flask/config.py#L172-L183>

### Expected behavior

Configuration loading should not fail with an implementation-level
`TypeError` for a prefix collision. The behavior should be defined and
deterministic, for example by rejecting the conflicting configuration with a
clear error, or by documenting and implementing precedence/merge semantics.

### Impact

An application can fail during startup or configuration initialization when
environment variables are assembled from multiple sources and a scalar key
and nested key happen to share a prefix. This can be difficult to diagnose
because the error does not identify the conflicting environment variables.

### Suggested regression test

Add a test covering both `FLASK_FOO=bar` and `FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz`, and assert the
chosen behavior for the scalar/nested conflict. If the intended behavior is to
reject the configuration, the error should identify the conflicting path.

### Environment

- Flask source commit: `6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`
- Flask version: `3.2.0.dev`
- Python: `3.13.13`
- Reproduction is independent of operating system semantics because it only
  relies on the environment-variable traversal logic.

I have not assigned a CWE classification. This is reported as a configuration
robustness and error-handling issue rather than a nullability finding.

issues.title: `stream_with_context`: abandoned generator leaves the app context current on the worker thread; later requests skip `teardown_appcontext`
issues.body:
`stream_with_context` pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. When a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later — often on a different thread. That cross-context pop fails (`LookupError`/`ValueError` from `ContextVar.reset`, swallowed as "Exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread.

Because `RequestContext.push` reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for it. Anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with Flask-SQLAlchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs.

Related: #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite. Neither covers the abandonment case. The docs mention that headers/session need care with `stream_with_context`, but not that a disconnect can leave the context stuck on the thread — a warning there would be helpful even if the behavior itself is hard to change.

## Reproduction

One long-lived "worker" thread serves two requests; the abandoned body iterator is GC-finalized on the main thread in between (in real deployments the reference is dropped by server machinery outside the worker — servers may never call `close()` on the iterator after a disconnect):

```python
import gc
import queue
import threading

from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context
from flask.globals import _cv_app

app = Flask(__name__)
teardowns = []

@app.teardown_appcontext
def note_teardown(exc):
    teardowns.append(threading.current_thread().name)

@app.route("/stream")
def stream():
    def gen():
        for i in range(100):
            yield f"chunk{i}\n"
    return Response(stream_with_context(gen()))

@app.route("/plain")
def plain():
    return "ok"

abandoned = queue.Queue()   # holds the dropped iterator, like server machinery
step2 = threading.Event()

def worker():
    # --- request A: streaming response, client disconnects after one chunk ---
    with app.test_request_context("/stream"):
        rv = app.full_dispatch_request()
    body = iter(rv.response)
    next(body)   # first chunk: stream_with_context pushes app+request ctx HERE
    abandoned.put((body, rv))   # server-side reference outlives the request
    del body, rv
    print("A: ambient ctx after abandonment:", _cv_app.get(None))

    step2.wait()  # main thread GC-finalizes the generator meanwhile

    # --- request B: any later request on this pooled worker thread ---
    print("B: ambient ctx at request start:", _cv_app.get(None))
    teardowns.clear()
    with app.test_request_context("/plain"):    # reuses the ambient ctx of the
        app.full_dispatch_request()             # same app -> no fresh app ctx
    print("B: teardown_appcontext ran for B:", bool(teardowns))
    print("B: ambient ctx after B finished:", _cv_app.get(None))

t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name="wsgi-worker-0")
t.start()

abandoned.get()          # take the reference, then drop it on the MAIN thread
gc.collect()             # generator finalized here -> cross-context pop fails
step2.set()
t.join()
```

Output (Flask 3.1.3, Python 3.13):

```
Exception ignored in: <generator object stream_with_context.<locals>.generator at 0x...>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../flask/helpers.py", line 130, in generator
    with app_ctx, req_ctx:
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 284, in __exit__
    self.pop(exc_value)
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 264, in pop
    ctx = _cv_app.get()
LookupError: <ContextVar name='flask.app_ctx' at 0x...>
A: ambient ctx after abandonment: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: ambient ctx at request start: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: teardown_appcontext ran for B: False
B: ambient ctx after B finished: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
```

## Expected behavior

Request B runs under its own app context and `teardown_appcontext` fires when it finishes. Instead it silently runs under request A's leaked context, teardown never runs, and the thread stays poisoned indefinitely.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13 (also reproduced on 3.11)
- Flask version: 3.1.3. The `main` branch (3.2-dev, post-#5639 merged context) looks affected as well: `stream_with_context` there enters the single context via `with ctx:` around the priming `yield None`, so the context is pushed at creation and only exited when the generator completes or is closed.

Sup! 
I'm sort of new to this open source contribution stuff and been looking for a contribution in a big project like this. 
Could I try on this one?

I don't think this is something for a new contributor. But you're welcome to read our contributing guide https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/ and AI policy https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/llm-ai and decide for yourself.

The example seems to require "server-side reference outlives the request", which seems extremely unusual. You're deliberately moving a reference from one thread to another, then reporting that the references act weird.

I would really prefer an example that uses a plain flask app and actual requests, rather than trying to simulate a bunch of stuff. There's so much complexity in the example right now that I'm having a hard time following it.

> the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later

This seems like something to report to the server doing this? They should be calling `close` on the iterator if it has that method. Otherwise they're creating an unclosed resource, something Python has been getting noisier and noisier about with warnings. If you look at Werkzeug's dev server and various app running functions, they all do this.

The app where I ran into this issue is an LLM gateway streaming chat responses from a generator that uses flask + SQLAlchemy/Postgres behind uvicorn (via a2wsgi). Under load I was slowly leaking 20–100 Postgres connections a day until I had to restart. 

 The trap: the streaming generator held a Flask app/request context across its yields, and a2wsgi iterates the response body on a reused thread-pool thread. When a client disconnected mid-stream the generator was abandoned, the context was never popped, and SQLAlchemy's per-context session teardown never ran. The database connection was stuck in "idle in transaction" (which I reaped before I found the issue by setting the postgresql idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 10min). Every later request that landed on that same thread reused the still-current context, so its session teardown never ran either. Each one quietly leaked another connection, which resulting the app loosing connections in the pool slowely and eventually crash, not immediatly.

> The trap:

Can you please re-post the issue in your own words without using an LLM to generate anything? See our LLM policy https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/llm-ai
Also, that response doesn't really answer my questions. It really seems like this needs to be reported to the server that's doing this, it's not behaving correctly.

Here is an example that is maybe better, flask, uvcorn, sqlalchemy and a2wsgi

```python
import os
import socket
import threading
import time

from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context
from flask.globals import _cv_app
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
from sqlalchemy.orm import scoped_session, sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.pool import QueuePool
from a2wsgi import WSGIMiddleware
import uvicorn

PORT = 8765
POOL_SIZE = 30

# sqlite database with connection pool
engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///./mydb.db",
    poolclass=QueuePool,
    pool_size=POOL_SIZE,
    max_overflow=0,
    connect_args={"check_same_thread": False},
)

# my flask app
app = Flask(__name__)
asgi_app = WSGIMiddleware(app, workers=16)

# code to keep track of connections
def _scope():
    ctx = _cv_app.get(None)
    return id(ctx) if ctx is not None else None

Session = scoped_session(sessionmaker(bind=engine), scopefunc=_scope)

@app.teardown_appcontext
def _cleanup(exc):
    # Flask runs this when the app context is popped. If the context is stranded
    # on a stuck worker thread, this never fires for it -> connection leaks.
    Session.remove()

# my generator to stream the answer back
def _tokens():
    # Open a session thens tream the result
    Session().execute(text("select 1")).all()
    for i in range(50):
        yield f"data: token {i}\n\n"
        time.sleep(0.05)

# endpoint that streams the result
@app.route("/stream")
def stream():
    return Response(stream_with_context(_tokens()), mimetype="text/event-stream")

# start serving the data
def _serve():
    uvicorn.run(asgi_app, host="127.0.0.1", port=PORT, log_level="critical")

# request data, wait a bit, break connection
def _abort_request():
    s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", PORT), timeout=5)
    s.sendall(
        b"GET /stream HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"
    )
    # set this to 1 == leak, 5 == no leak
    time.sleep(1)             # let the stream start and a few tokens flow
    s.recv(256)               # read a little
    s.close()                 # disconnect mid-stream -> abandons the generator

def main():
    # start the flask app
    threading.Thread(target=_serve, daemon=True).start()
    time.sleep(2)

    # start the clients
    print(f"{'batch':>6} {'checked_out':>12} {'live sessions':>14}")
    for batch in range(1, 6):
        threads = [threading.Thread(target=_abort_request) for _ in range(20)]
        for t in threads:
            t.start()
        for t in threads:
            t.join()
        time.sleep(1)
        checked_out = engine.pool.checkedout()
        live_sessions = len(Session.registry.registry)
        print(f"{batch:>6} {checked_out:>12} {live_sessions:>14}")

    print(
        "\nLEAK" if engine.pool.checkedout() > 0
        else "\nno leak — connections all returned"
    )
    checked_out = engine.pool.checkedout()
    live_sessions = len(Session.registry.registry)
    print(f"{batch:>6} {checked_out:>12} {live_sessions:>14}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Sorry, that's still way too much. I can't debug a2wsgi, I'm not familiar with it at all, if you think it's causing issues then report that to them. Use Flask's dev server, it's threaded. It doesn't seem like sqlalchemy is necessary at all to demonstrate that contexts aren't cleaned up.

I've been looking into this for hours now, and as far as I can tell the problem is that something is not closing the response. Flask _can't_ do that, it's in the server's control at that point.

In your first example, you're never calling `body.close()` when the "connection" is disconnected, and you're deliberately moving it somewhere with a different `contextvar`. If you call `body.close()` in the worker (not in some other thread) it works fine.

In your second example, presumably a2wsgi isn't handling client disconnects correctly, it needs to detect them and close the response.

It seems like Flask is managing the context correctly but your server is not handling disconnects correctly. How should a2wsgi do that? I don't know, but I'd suggest you report it to them.

issues.body:
## Description

When a client disconnects mid-stream, the WSGI server abandons the body
iterator. The generator is later finalized by the garbage collector, often
on a **different thread** than the one that pushed the context.

`ctx.pop()` raises `RuntimeError` because `_cv_app.get(None)` returns `None`
on the GC thread. The context stays "stuck" on the original worker thread,
and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for subsequent requests on that thread.

## Fix

Replace `with ctx:` with manual `ctx.push()` / `ctx.pop()` in the
`stream_with_context` generator. Wrap `pop()` in a try/except that catches
`RuntimeError` and resets the context state (`_push_count` and `_cv_token`)
to prevent thread pool poisoning.

## Related

- #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views
- #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite

Closes #6123

### Subject

`BytesQueueBuffer.get()` is slow when downloading gzipped, unchunked data.

By profiling with `line_profiler`, I identified the slowest part in the `BytesQueueBuffer.get()`, specifically the following line:
https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b20c8368ec02421ecc4e49d796cd5eff1e04f325/src/urllib3/response.py#L259

### Environment

```
OS Linux-6.12.48-1-MANJARO-x86_64-with-glibc2.42
Python 3.12.5
OpenSSL 3.0.14 4 Jun 2024
urllib3 0.1.dev4309
```

I also confirmed this with python 3.14.

As this is a performance issue, I will put the CPU and memory info just in case:
```
CPU: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-13500

> free
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           31833       11164       15246        1254        7134       20669
Swap:              0           0           0
```

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone https://gist.github.com/phenylshima/0af2d0692db455d2d040805289689fef
2. Install `urllib3==2.5.0`, `fastapi==0.121.1`, and `uvicorn==0.38.0`
3. Start test_server.py
4. Run test_client.py, and check the "Content retrieval time" line.

### Expected Behavior

The two "Content retrieval time" are almost the same.

### Actual Behavior

Content retrieval time is about 9x slower when decode_content=True, compared to taking the whole data with decode_content=False and then unzipping.

```
Response time: 0.001905202865600586 seconds
Content retrieval time: 2.0758426189422607 seconds
Response time: 0.0009431838989257812 seconds
Content retrieval and decompression time: 0.2243025302886963 seconds
```

nodes.body:
FYI, we did further improvements in c19571de34c47de3a766541b041637ba5f716ed7.

Benchmarks for the following script reading 32 KiB chunks of a 1 GiB response

```python
from compression import zstd
import io
import timeit

from urllib3.response import HTTPResponse


data = b"A" * (1024 * 1024 * 1024)  # 1 GB
compressed_data = zstd.ZstdCompressor().compress(data)


def decompress():
    fp = io.BytesIO(compressed_data)
    r = HTTPResponse(fp, headers={"content-encoding": "zstd"}, preload_content=False)
    while r.read(32 * 1024):
        pass

time_taken = timeit.timeit(decompress, number=10)
print(f"Decompression time: {time_taken:.2f} seconds")
```

Results:
* Before 18af0a10efc4c99dd028f7ad5a461470b9a8b0fd – even one `decompress()` call did not finish under a minute. It decompressed 1 GB during the first `read` call and then `BytesQueueBuffer.get` was splitting chunks by creating copies of the data which was extremely slow.
* 18af0a10efc4c99dd028f7ad5a461470b9a8b0fd – 13.69 seconds for ten `decompress()` calls
* c19571de34c47de3a766541b041637ba5f716ed7 – 0.66 seconds for ten `decompress()` calls

issues.title: Improve speed of `BytesQueueBuffer.get()` by using memoryview
issues.body:
Fixes #3710

This pull request improves the speed of `BytesQueueBuffer.get()` by using memoryview, solving the problem described in #3710 .

nodes.body:
Does it make more sense to just always store the byte chunks as memoryviews? My instinct was that would solve this as well. 

We'll need to update the type hints as well as now the deque can have either bytes or memoryview probably
@sigmavirus24 Thank you for your suggestion! I updated the code to store the data as memoryview.
Is that as performant at least?

Yes, at least on my machine.

Test code:
```py
from src.urllib3.response import BytesQueueBuffer
import time

buffer = BytesQueueBuffer()
buffer.put(b"x" * 1024 * 1024 * 10)  # 10 MiB
now = time.perf_counter()
while len(buffer) > 5000:
    buffer.get(1024)  # 1 KiB
delta = time.perf_counter() - now

print(delta)
```

The result:
[495aab1](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3711/commits/495aab1bd0e74cc485d7790ba7132802fbfebc3c): 0.0052835239985142834
[19820a4](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3711/commits/19820a42035b7ce266da1f9792f515027a733c41): 0.004722315999970306

The new one looks faster, but it is because the `memoryview(chunk)` is moved to `put` method. I think the overall performance is the same. One thing to note is when we write a big chunk once, and read it only once (either by get or get_all), I expect it to be slightly slower compared to the current main branch (due to running `memoryview(chunk)` and converting it back to `bytes`. If get_all is used, the conversion back to bytes will not happen though).

Worth checking for a performance hit on `.put` then from before your changes to now then, although I don't expect much of one. May as well also do a full end-to-end performance test. Put a bunch of chunks, do a `get_all`, etc.

I tested in the original repro, and it looked fine.

However, the `put` method got slower (surprising to me):

```py
from src.urllib3.response import BytesQueueBuffer
import time

buffer = BytesQueueBuffer()
now = time.perf_counter()

for _ in range(10 * 1024):  # 10 MiB total
    buffer.put(b"x" * 1024)  # 1 KiB

delta = time.perf_counter() - now
print(f"Time to put data: {delta}s")

while len(buffer) > 0:
    buffer.get(1024)  # 1 KiB

delta = time.perf_counter() - now

print(f"Time to get data: {delta}s")
```

```
> ~/dev/urllib3> main !1 ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007599639998261409s
Time to get data: 0.004324924999764335s
> ~/dev/urllib3> main !1 ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0008291090002785495s
Time to get data: 0.004370479000044725s
> ~/dev/urllib3> main !1 ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007629809997524717s
Time to get data: 0.004293366999718273s

> ~/dev/urllib3> @495aab1b ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007698970002820715s
Time to get data: 0.004365679000329692s
> ~/dev/urllib3> @495aab1b ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.000990569999885338s
Time to get data: 0.004518313000062335s
> ~/dev/urllib3> @495aab1b ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0009582410002622055s
Time to get data: 0.004823216000204411s

> ~/dev/urllib3> byte-queue-perf ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.003418835000047693s
Time to get data: 0.007445904999713093s
> ~/dev/urllib3> byte-queue-perf ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0033251579998250236s
Time to get data: 0.007321049999973184s
> ~/dev/urllib3> byte-queue-perf ?1> python t.py
Time to put data: 0.003460155999619019s
Time to get data: 0.00736400899995715s
```

Maybe because this code is not reveraging anything from bytes->memoryview conversion, as it is just reading and writing the same size?

It might be better to use 495aab1b.

Now it's like this:
```
>~/dev/urllib3 > byte-queue-perf ?1 > python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007707550003033248s
Time to get data: 0.004282103000150528s
>~/dev/urllib3 > byte-queue-perf ?1 > python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007912390001365566s
Time to get data: 0.004329170999881171s
>~/dev/urllib3 > byte-queue-perf ?1 > python t.py
Time to put data: 0.0007524289994762512s
Time to get data: 0.004279935999875306s
```
Am I misreading the benchmarks? I'm not seeing a speed difference between `main` and the last `byte-queue-perf` benchmark: 0.7ms for put and 4ms for get.

Thank you for looking at this PR. The current test does not test the execution time, rather the non-existance of extra memory allocation (that led to the overhead in the current main branch).
Changing `buffer.get(2**20)` to `buffer.get(2**10)` or something like that should make the performance difference more visible (I'm not sure if I should commit it, though).

I believe Quentin asked about the benchmarks from https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3711#issuecomment-3530483296 and https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3711#issuecomment-3533040535 which did not measure the effect of using `memoryview` for chunks that are split.

The benchmarked case was related to a regression that was introduced by this PR initially and has been resolved since then in e898682a2ba0ef1e1205366a48d789f63cf3ec58: memoryview was used even when a chunk was not split.
Ah I see, thank you for the followup!

issues.body: `test/port_helpers.py` is a copy of https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/test/support/socket_helper.py from CPython 3.9. We should upgrade it to a more recent version, likely Python 3.14, while keeping our own changes if relevant.

nodes.body: Hello, I would like to work on this. I'm planning to start on it tomorrow.

@pquentin 
I have done some research into this and here are my findings.

1. port_helpers.py only uses the `find_unused_port` and `bind_port` functions from socket_helper.py. 
2. There are a number of changes between 3.9 and 3.14.0 in socket_helper.py, but the only change in the 2 functions used in port_helpers.py is a link in the docstring which is changed to the URL where it redirects anyway. There are some new imports and a new variable related to WASI but they are not used in the 2 functions.

issues.title: Fix for issue #3636 around read() after partial read not returning full content
issues.body:
#3636 

This issue was, `read(512)`
- Reads the entire compressed stream from the socket
- Decompresses it
- Returns only the requested 512 bytes
- Stores the rest in `_decoded_buffer`

But when doing `read()` after, it would only try and read from the socket and ignore the buffered decoded data.

Now when `amt=None` we check if `_decoded_buffer` has leftover data

nodes.body:
Sure, we've now got a specific single exception for mixed `decode_content` in `read()`.

This is already tested by existing test `test_response::test_read_with_illegal_mix_decode_toggle`.

And now setting the `cache_content` to false when doing a partial read (can't cache incomplete data)
The new tests from this PR no longer reveal the issue on the main branch and the suggested fix is not complete, I'm closing this PR in favor of #4960

issues.title: Update ConnectionPool Queue to support gevent monkey_patch
issues.body:
Fix for #3289 

Do late binding of `queue.LifeQueue` via a metaclass that allows it intercept accesses to `QueueCls` and delay the import of `queue` until then.

You can test the behaviour like this. I've not added this as a new test yet, because there's currently no gevent tests and it's a bit different to other tests. Happy to add this as a test if it makes sense in the urllib3 test suite.

``` python
import urllib3
from urllib3.connectionpool import HTTPConnectionPool

print("Before monkey-patch:")
print(f"  QueueCls: {HTTPConnectionPool.QueueCls}")
print(f"  Module: {HTTPConnectionPool.QueueCls.__module__}")

# Now monkey-patch (we only care about queue, not events)
import gevent.monkey
gevent.monkey.patch_queue()

print("\nAfter monkey-patch:")
print(f"  QueueCls: {HTTPConnectionPool.QueueCls}")
print(f"  Module: {HTTPConnectionPool.QueueCls.__module__}")

import queue
print(f"\nWhat queue.LifoQueue points to now:")
print(f"  queue.LifoQueue: {queue.LifoQueue}")
print(f"  Module: {queue.LifoQueue.__module__}")
```

issues.title: Brotli DecodeError with chunked transfer encoding: "can_accept_more_data() is False"
issues.body:
### Subject

When receiving a large brotli-compressed response with chunked transfer encoding, urllib3 2.6.x raises a `DecodeError` with the message:

```
brotli: decoder process called with data when 'can_accept_more_data()' is False
```

This appears to be a regression introduced in urllib3 2.6.0, likely related to the security changes for handling compressed content (GHSA-2xpw-w6gg-jr37). The issue occurs specifically when:
1. The response uses `Content-Encoding: br` (brotli)
2. The response uses `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
3. The compressed data is moderately large (~500KB+ compressed)
4. Data arrives in small TCP segments

The issue does **not** occur with urllib3 2.5.0.

### Environment

```
OS: Linux 6.x (Debian Bookworm in Docker)
Python: 3.12.12
OpenSSL: OpenSSL 3.0.x
urllib3: 2.6.1
brotli: 1.2.0
requests: 2.31.0
```

Works correctly with:
```
urllib3: 2.5.0
brotli: 1.1.0
```

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal reproduction script:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal reproduction: brotli decode bug with urllib3 2.6.x + brotli 1.2.0"""

import hashlib
import socket
import threading

import brotli
import requests


def main() -> int:
    from importlib.metadata import version

    print(f"urllib3: {version('urllib3')}, brotli: {version('brotli')}")

    # Generate ~15MB data with moderate compressibility (~27x ratio)
    data = b"".join(
        f"{hashlib.sha256(str(i).encode()).hexdigest()}{'a' * 900}{i:06d}\n".encode()
        for i in range(15000)
    )
    compressed = brotli.compress(data)
    print(f"Data: {len(data):,} -> {len(compressed):,} bytes ({len(data) // len(compressed)}x)")

    # Build chunked HTTP response
    resp = b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Encoding: br\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"
    for i in range(0, len(compressed), 32768):
        chunk = compressed[i : i + 32768]
        resp += f"{len(chunk):x}\r\n".encode() + chunk + b"\r\n"
    resp += b"0\r\n\r\n"

    # Start mock server
    ready = threading.Event()

    def serve(port: int) -> None:
        s = socket.socket()
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
        s.listen(1)
        ready.set()
        c, _ = s.accept()
        c.recv(4096)
        for i in range(0, len(resp), 128):  # Small chunks trigger bug
            c.send(resp[i : i + 128])
        c.close()
        s.close()

    threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(18765,), daemon=True).start()
    ready.wait()

    try:
        r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:18765/", timeout=60)
        print(f"SUCCESS: {len(r.content):,} bytes")
        return 0
    except requests.exceptions.ContentDecodingError as e:
        print(f"FAILED: {e}")
        return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    exit(main())
```

### Expected Behavior

The response should be successfully decompressed and returned:

```
urllib3: 2.5.0, brotli: 1.1.0
Data: 14,565,000 -> 549,724 bytes (26x)
SUCCESS: 14,565,000 bytes
```

### Actual Behavior

With urllib3 2.6.x, the request fails with a `ContentDecodingError`:

```
urllib3: 2.6.1, brotli: 1.2.0
Data: 14,565,000 -> 549,724 bytes (26x)
FAILED: ('Received response with content-encoding: br, but failed to decode it.', 
         error("brotli: decoder process called with data when 'can_accept_more_data()' is False"))
```

Full traceback:
```
urllib3.exceptions.DecodeError: ('Received response with content-encoding: br, but 
failed to decode it.', error("brotli: decoder process called with data when 
'can_accept_more_data()' is False"))
```

The error suggests that the brotli decoder signals completion (`can_accept_more_data()` returns `False`) but urllib3 continues trying to feed it more compressed data from the chunked stream.

issues.title: Handle massive values in Retry-After when calculating time to sleep for
issues.body:
The method `Retry.parse_retry_after(...)` will accept any integer returned by the remote server in the `Retry-After` header when the server returns a number of seconds to delay for rather than an HTTP-date. This includes massive and invalid values, for example `Retry-After: 9999999999`. This value is passed back to `Retry.sleep_for_retry(...)` which then uses the value directly in `time.sleep(...)`. The type is checked but not the value.

Using values for `time.sleep(...)` that exceed `PyTime_MAX` results in an OverflowError being raised:

```python
>>> time.sleep(9999999999)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-3>", line 1, in <module>
    time.sleep(9999999999)
    ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^
OverflowError: timestamp too large to convert to C PyTime_t
```

This minimal PR adds a sanity check to confirm that the value of the `Retry-After` header is < 2147483647 (2 ** 31 - 1) in value. While `PyTime_MAX` is a `INT64_MAX` this is still a relatively sane upper bound value. If the value exceeds 2147483647 a clearer and more descriptive exception is raised.

This issue was seen in the wild:

https://github.com/meeb/whoisit/issues/60

It's highly unlikely that actually sleeping for decades or centuries is desirable but that's a different issue. I don't believe there's a specified sensible maximum for `Retry-After` in the RFC, perhaps limiting this to `3600` or similar lower value would be sensible?

Currently, even with this PR, a semi-malicious server could add `if ($http_user_agent ~ urllib3) { add_header retry-after 5000000000; }` and lock up some clients that attempt to handle retries properly for over a century (or at least until the process gets killed).

nodes.body:
Reasonable suggestions. I've reworked it so the value is configurable and added a basic test in the format of the other tests. The magic number is currently set statically as `2_147_483_648` but with a comment as to why it's that value. I'm not a big fan of magic numbers in Python either, however this is the value used internally by CPython (at least in 32bit builds anyway) that when exceeded triggers the `OverflowError`. If this is just a sanity check feature this is the value it should be.

I don't mind adding an additional `if retry_after > x: retry_after = x` limit feature to stop remote sites from triggering `sleep(...)` for retries over a specific amount of time as a different PR, but that would likely require some discussion on what `x` should be first.

> I don't mind adding an additional `if retry_after > x: retry_after = x` limit feature to stop remote sites from triggering `sleep(...)` for retries over a specific amount of time as a different PR, but that would likely require some discussion on what `x` should be first.

I should clarify that I meant the suggested limit to be used either for capping the header value or for raising an error if it is too big.

I can see that curl limits `Retry-After` to 6 hours, the limit is pretty sensible
https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/6d0ee7b17b0c37c034a78314eda4148104187689/lib/http.c#L3446-L3449
https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/15833

We won't need to check whether it is less than `PyTime_t` in this case.
Yep that sounds sensible, thanks for picking `x`! I've removed the `PyTime_t` magic and this now just limits the headers to 6 hours without raising `InvalidHeader` as suggested.
Thanks for the review. I'll adjust as requested in a couple of days.
Your suggested changes have been made, this should be good to go.

issues.body:
<!---
Thanks for your contribution! ♥️

If this is your first PR to urllib3 please review the Contributing Guide:
https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing.html

Adhering to the Contributing Guide means we can review, merge, and release your change faster! :)
--->

Opening this as a suggestion and for discussion.

This PR:

* Reinstates the warnings removed in [#3732](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3732)
* Promotes from `DeprecationWarning` to `FutureWarning`
* Sets an arbitrary removal version of 2.7.0, can of course be adjusted (although I recommend advertising a target version)

Part of the problem with the earlier removal (https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3731) was, despite years of `DeprecationWarning`, many projects had not noticed and acted upon the warnings.

[`DeprecationWarning`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#DeprecationWarning) is often hidden:

> Base class for warnings about deprecated features when those warnings are intended for other Python developers.
> 
> Ignored by the default warning filters, except in the __main__ module ([PEP 565](https://peps.python.org/pep-0565/)). Enabling the [Python Development Mode](https://docs.python.org/3/library/devmode.html#devmode) shows this warning.

However, one of @sethmlarson's suggestions in https://sethmlarson.dev/deprecations-via-warnings-dont-work-for-python-libraries is for projects to create their own warning class like `Urllib3DeprecationWarning(UserWarning)`, which would be more visible.

Another suggestion is to use [`FutureWarning`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#FutureWarning):

> Base class for warnings about deprecated features when those warnings are intended for end users of applications that are written in Python.

This would be more visible to users of urllib3, with the hope they will finally take action and update their code.

issues.title: Bug Report
issues.body:
_Environment used for validation_: Python 3.12 virtualenv at `.venv` with `urllib3==2.6.2` (latest on PyPI) plus optional `h2==4.3.0`.

## Findings

### 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/response.py:619`-`src/urllib3/response.py:1110`
- **Impact:** When `Accept-Encoding` is enabled (default), `HTTPResponse.read()` always fully inflates compressed bodies without any upper bound on the decoded size. A malicious peer can send a very small gzip/brotli/zstd payload that expands to gigabytes, leading to client-side memory exhaustion or process termination, independent of the advertised `Content-Length`.
- **Details:** `_decode()` forces `max_length=-1` when `flush_decoder` is true (line 637) and directly feeds all incoming bytes to the decoder (line 641) while `read()` keeps appending to `_decoded_buffer` until the requested amount is satisfied or EOF (line 1097 onward). There is no limit tied to `Content-Length`, streaming hint, or caller-provided cap, so any compressed response is eagerly expanded into RAM.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (50 * 1024 * 1024))  # 50 MB after inflate

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/")
  print(len(resp.data))  # prints 52428800, showing the inflated size held in memory

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Increasing the payload size proportionally increases instantaneous memory usage in the urllib3 client process.
- **Recommendation:** Introduce configurable limits for the decoded body size (e.g., cap based on `Content-Length`, a new `max_decoded_bytes` parameter, or stop inflating once a threshold is hit) and allow streaming decoders to hand off chunks directly to the caller without buffering everything in `_decoded_buffer`.

### 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`
- **Impact:** When `Retry.respect_retry_after_header` (True by default) is set, urllib3 trusts any `Retry-After` header and performs `time.sleep(retry_after)` with the parsed value. A malicious origin or intermediary can respond with `Retry-After: 31536000` to block the caller’s worker thread for a year, bypassing request-level timeouts and causing denial of service across thread pools.
- **Details:** `sleep_for_retry()` parses either a delta seconds or HTTP-date (lines 308-323) and, if present, unconditionally calls `time.sleep(retry_after)` (line 338) before reattempting the request. There is no upper bound, no linkage to the configured timeout, and no way to abort the sleep other than thread interruption.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import http.server, socketserver, threading, time
  import urllib3

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(503)
          self.send_header("Retry-After", "5")  # attacker controls this value
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *args):
          pass

  server = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  retries = urllib3.util.retry.Retry(total=1, respect_retry_after_header=True)
  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  try:
      http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_address[1]}/", retries=retries)
  except urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError:
      pass
  print(round(time.time() - start, 2))  # ~5.0 seconds, equal to Retry-After header

  server.shutdown()
  ```
  Raising the header to hours or days will stall the thread for the same duration.
- **Recommendation:** Cap `Retry-After` sleeps to a configurable maximum (defaulting to a few seconds) or tie the sleep to the original request timeout; allow users to opt out or enforce asynchronous cancellation.

### 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False` (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-266` and `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:324-347`
- **Impact:** The experimental HTTP/2 backend accumulates the entire response body in a `bytearray` (line 230) and materializes it into `HTTP2Response.data` regardless of the caller’s `preload_content` flag. There is no streaming API, so any large HTTP/2 download forces full buffering, opening the door to memory exhaustion when a remote server (or CDN) sends multi-GB responses. Dependent services expecting streaming semantics (e.g., `stream=True` in requests) silently lose back-pressure when HTTP/2 is enabled.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.getresponse()` reads until `StreamEnded`, appending each `DataReceived` chunk to `data` (lines 248-255). The resulting bytes are stored in `_data` inside `HTTP2Response` (line 331), and methods such as `.stream()` are not implemented. The passed `preload_content` flag from `HTTPSConnectionPool.urlopen()` is ignored entirely for HTTP/2 connections.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  http = urllib3.PoolManager(headers={"accept-encoding": "identity"})
  resp = http.request(
      "GET",
      "https://nghttp2.org/httpbin/stream-bytes/10240",
      preload_content=False,
  )
  print(resp.version_string, len(resp.data))  # -> HTTP/2 10240
  urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  ```
  Despite `preload_content=False`, the full payload is buffered in `resp.data`. Increasing the endpoint size quickly spikes RAM.
- **Recommendation:** Honor `preload_content=False` by exposing a streaming HTTP/2 response object (e.g., forward `DataReceived` frames to an iterator) or block HTTP/2 upgrades unless the caller explicitly opts in to buffering. At a minimum, document the limitation and provide safeguards (max buffered bytes) to prevent accidental memory exhaustion.

### 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies (High)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:503` and `src/urllib3/response.py:793`-`src/urllib3/response.py:801`
- **Impact:** When a response triggers a redirect, `PoolManager` always calls `response.drain_conn()` before following the `Location`. `drain_conn()` simply invokes `HTTPResponse.read()` with default arguments, which eagerly inflates any `Content-Encoding` on the response body. An attacker can reply with `302 Found`, a tiny compressed payload that expands to hundreds of megabytes, and a benign `Location`. The client must fully decompress the unused body before the redirect is honored, leading to CPU and memory exhaustion without the application ever touching the response object.
- **Details:** The redirect logic at `poolmanager.py:500-503` calls `response.drain_conn()` unconditionally. `drain_conn()` in turn calls `self.read()` (response.py:799-800), which performs the same unlimited decompression described in Finding 1. Because redirects are handled internally, even a single GET to an attacker-controlled URL can force the client to inflate arbitrary amounts of data just to reach the next hop.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import gzip, http.server, socketserver, threading, time, urllib3

  payload = gzip.compress(b"A" * (200 * 1024 * 1024))  # ~200 MB once inflated

  class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          if self.path == "/next":
              self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok")
              return
          self.send_response(302)
          self.send_header("Location", "/next")
          self.send_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(payload)
      def log_message(self, *args): pass

  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
  threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

  http = urllib3.PoolManager()
  start = time.time()
  resp = http.request("GET", f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/")
  print(resp.status, resp.data, "elapsed", round(time.time() - start, 2), "s")
  srv.shutdown()
  ```
  Even though the redirect target is only “ok”, the client spends noticeable time decompressing the 200 MB payload. Scaling the compressed bomb quickly leads to out-of-memory conditions.
- **Recommendation:** Avoid decompressing or even reading redirect bodies entirely—most clients ignore them. At minimum, cap the number of bytes that `drain_conn()` will pull (both raw and decoded) or skip draining compressed redirect bodies by closing the socket instead of decompressing attacker data.

### 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers (Medium)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:616` and `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477`-`src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:487`
- **Impact:** When using a plain HTTP proxy (no CONNECT), urllib3 mis-identifies every redirect as “cross-host” because `ProxyManager.connection_from_host()` builds pools keyed on the proxy host (line 614). Consequently `conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` always returns `False`, so the redirect logic strips every header listed in `Retry.remove_headers_on_redirect`—including `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and any user-provided entries—even if the redirect stays on the exact same origin. Authenticated HTTP workflows behind proxies therefore lose credentials or session cookies after the first redirect and often fall into infinite login loops.
- **Details:** For HTTP destinations, `connection_from_host()` ignores the target host and instead returns a pool for `self.proxy.host` (`poolmanager.py:614-616`). Later, `PoolManager.urlopen()` removes “unsafe” headers whenever `not conn.is_same_host(redirect_location)` (`poolmanager.py:477-487`). Because `conn.host` is the proxy, not the origin, this condition is always true and every redirect is treated as cross-origin.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://proxy.local:8080")
  conn = proxy.connection_from_host("example.com", 80, "http")
  print("pool host:", conn.host)  # -> proxy.local
  print("same host redirect?",
        conn.is_same_host("http://example.com/secure"))  # -> False
  ```
  The above means cookies/Authorization headers will be stripped before following even a relative redirect to `/secure`. Users behind mandatory HTTP proxies cannot stay authenticated on any site that issues redirects (OAuth, SSO, login flows).
- **Recommendation:** Track the original destination host separately from the proxy host when evaluating `is_same_host` for redirects, or short-circuit the removal logic when a forwarding proxy is in use so headers are only stripped when the *destination* host truly changes.

### 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright (Low)
- **Location:** `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94`-`src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:103` and `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30`-`src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:42`
- **Impact:** Calling `urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()` replaces every `HTTPSConnection` with `HTTP2Connection`, which explicitly raises `NotImplementedError` whenever `proxy` or `proxy_config` is supplied. Any deployment that uses proxies (corporate networks, tests that rely on mitmproxy, etc.) immediately loses outbound HTTPS support once HTTP/2 is injected, effectively taking the client offline.
- **Details:** `HTTP2Connection.__init__` rejects all proxy kwargs (line 94) and the injector rewires `HTTPSConnectionPool.ConnectionCls` globally to `HTTP2Connection` (http2/__init__.py lines 30-36). Proxied requests therefore crash before any network traffic is attempted.
- **Proof of Concept:**
  ```python
  import urllib3, urllib3.http2

  urllib3.http2.inject_into_urllib3()
  proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://127.0.0.1:3128/")
  try:
      proxy.request("GET", "https://example.com/", timeout=urllib3.util.Timeout(1))
  except Exception as exc:
      print(type(exc).__name__, exc)
  finally:
      urllib3.http2.extract_from_urllib3()
  # -> NotImplementedError: Proxies aren't supported with HTTP/2
  ```
- **Recommendation:** Either keep HTTP/1.1 as a fallback ALPN option when proxies are present or block the injection entirely when proxy settings are detected so that enabling HTTP/2 cannot silently break every proxied request.

## Summary

| #   | Title                                                         | Location                                                                        | Severity |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| 1   | Unlimited decompression grows unbounded client memory         | `src/urllib3/response.py:619-1110`                                              | High     |
| 2   | `Retry-After` header can stall threads indefinitely           | `src/urllib3/util/retry.py:308-339`                                             | Medium   |
| 3   | HTTP/2 responses ignore streaming hints and buffer entirely   | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:226-347`                                       | Medium   |
| 4   | Redirect draining decompresses attacker-controlled bodies     | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:500-503`, `src/urllib3/response.py:793-801`         | High     |
| 5   | HTTP proxies treat every redirect as cross-host and drop auth | `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:477-487`, `src/urllib3/poolmanager.py:602-616`      | Medium   |
| 6   | Global HTTP/2 injection disables all proxied HTTPS traffic    | `src/urllib3/http2/connection.py:94-103`, `src/urllib3/http2/__init__.py:30-42` | Low      |

nodes.body:
Hi @D47A,

Thanks for the report! However, we'd appreciate if you reported potential security vulnerabilities privately using our security contact mentioned in [our Security Policy](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/security/policy).

> 1. Unlimited decompression can exhaust client memory

We are aware of the issue, but we do not consider it a vulnerability.
urllib3's users are advised to use [the streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o)  when dealing with responses of large or unknown length including responses from untrusted sources.

FYI, we applied a security hardening to the streaming API in the recent 2.6.0 release, check GHSA-2xpw-w6gg-jr37.

While unlimited decompression by the non-streaming API is not a security issue due to the described reasons, we consider adding parameters for configuring the maximum allowed response size as a new feature.


> 2. `Retry-After` header induces unbounded client sleep

Duplicate of #3743, fixed in 2.6.3


> 3. HTTP/2 responses are always fully buffered despite `preload_content=False`

It is fine to report HTTP/2 issues publicly because it is an experimental and uncomplete functionality.
#3300 exists for adding support for streaming HTTP/2 responses.


> 4. Redirect draining eagerly decompresses attacker-controlled bodies

This is a valid security issue, fixed in 2.6.3, see GHSA-38jv-5279-wg99


> 5. HTTP proxy redirects always drop `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers

I am not inclined to accept this as a security issue since the confidential information is not passed to third parties, but the issue does sound like a bug.


> 6. Enabling HTTP/2 globally makes proxy usage fail outright

#3299 exists for adding support for proxies with HTTP/2.

> I also noticed that `EmscriptenHTTPConnection` doesn't have the `response_class` property, another property that `botocore` relies on existing. What should that be set to?

Does it work with `response_class = EmscriptenHttpResponseWrapper`?

> > I also noticed that `EmscriptenHTTPConnection` doesn't have the `response_class` property, another property that `botocore` relies on existing. What should that be set to?
> 
> Does it work with `response_class = EmscriptenHttpResponseWrapper`?



> > I also noticed that `EmscriptenHTTPConnection` doesn't have the `response_class` property, another property that `botocore` relies on existing. What should that be set to?
> 
> Does it work with `response_class = EmscriptenHttpResponseWrapper`?

That sounds correct!

`botocore` doesn't actually do anything with the property other than backing it up and restoring it (so I was able to patch in `None` and the code worked), but given that `response_class` should be the class that is returned by `getresponse`, and we return a `EmscriptenHttpResponseWrapper` there, this makes sense.

issues.title: Add comprehensive Hypothesis property-based testing suite for urllib3
issues.body:
This PR introduces a comprehensive property-based testing suite using the Hypothesis framework, adding extensive test coverage for core urllib3 modules including connection handling, URL parsing, field encoding, request/response processing, retry logic, and timeout mechanisms.

### Changes

- **Added Hypothesis test files**:
  - `test/test_hypothesis_connection.py` - Property-based tests for connection utilities and HTTP tunnel logic
  - `test/test_hypothesis_fields.py` - Property-based tests for request field formatting and encoding
  - `test/test_hypothesis_headers.py` - Property-based tests for HTTP header handling and validation
  - `test/test_hypothesis_request.py` - Property-based tests for request encoding and body handling
  - `test/test_hypothesis_response.py` - Property-based tests for response decoding and stream processing
  - `test/test_hypothesis_retry.py` - Property-based tests for retry logic and backoff strategies
  - `test/test_hypothesis_timeout.py` - Property-based tests for timeout configurations
  - `test/test_hypothesis_url.py` - Property-based tests for URL parsing, encoding, and manipulation

### What is Hypothesis?

**Hypothesis** is an advanced property-based testing framework for Python that automatically generates test cases to find edge cases and bugs that traditional example-based tests might miss. Instead of manually writing specific test examples, you describe the *properties* that your code should satisfy, and Hypothesis generates hundreds of test inputs to verify those properties hold true.

### Why is Hypothesis useful?

1. **Discovers edge cases automatically**: Hypothesis generates diverse test inputs including boundary values, empty collections, special characters, and unusual combinations that developers often overlook when writing manual tests.

2. **Reduces test maintenance**: Instead of maintaining dozens of individual test cases, you write a single property-based test that covers a wide range of scenarios, making tests more concise and maintainable.

3. **Provides reproducible failures**: When Hypothesis finds a failing test case, it automatically minimizes the input to the simplest example that reproduces the bug and saves it for future test runs.

4. **Increases confidence**: By testing against randomly generated inputs, property-based tests provide stronger guarantees about code correctness across a broader input space than fixed example tests.

5. **Catches regressions**: Hypothesis remembers previously-found edge cases and includes them in future test runs, ensuring bugs don't reappear.

6. **Integrates with fuzzing tools**: Hypothesis works seamlessly with **[HypoFuzz](https://hypofuzz.com/)**, an adaptive fuzzing tool that extends Hypothesis tests with coverage-guided fuzzing. HypoFuzz can run continuously in CI/CD pipelines to discover deep bugs that might only appear after millions of test executions, providing an additional layer of security and reliability testing.

For the urllib3 library specifically, Hypothesis helps ensure robust handling of various URL formats, header combinations, connection configurations, retry scenarios, timeout values, and response data structures that users might provide in real-world scenarios.

### Testing

All new Hypothesis tests pass and can be run with:
```bash
pytest test/test_hypothesis_*.py
```

To run with more examples for deeper testing:
```bash
pytest test/test_hypothesis_*.py --hypothesis-profile=thorough
```

issues.title: Remove Python 3.9 support (EOL) and modernize codebase for Python 3.10+
issues.body:
Removes support for Python 3.9 (which reached end-of-life) and updates the minimum supported Python version to 3.10. This change allows us to clean up legacy workarounds and modernize the codebase.

## Changes

### Configuration & CI
- Updated `pyproject.toml` to require Python >=3.10
- Removed Python 3.9 classifier from package metadata
- Removed Python 3.9 from CI workflow test matrix
- Removed Python 3.9 specific integration test for SSL workaround
- Updated `noxfile.py` to exclude Python 3.9 from test sessions

### Documentation
- Updated migration guide to reflect Python 3.10+ requirement
- Updated contributing guide to remove Python 3.9 references
- Corrected version references throughout documentation

### Code Modernization
- Removed Python 3.9.3 SSL hostname checking workarounds (`ssl_.py`)
- Removed IPv6 scoped address workaround that was needed for Python <3.9 (`ssl_match_hostname.py`)
- Adopted parenthesized context managers (Python 3.10+ feature) in tests
- Cleaned up defensive code and comments for Python 3.9 limitations
- Removed CPython <3.9.7 bug workaround in `response.py`

## Impact

- **Breaking Change**: Python 3.9 is no longer supported
- Users must upgrade to Python 3.10 or later
- Codebase is cleaner with fewer version-specific workarounds
- Better alignment with modern Python practices

issues.title: Switch deprecation warnings to `FutureWarning` and reschedule removals
issues.body:
The codebase contains a few deprecation warnings with unmet target versions.
We've recently discovered that warnings using `DeprecationWarning` were not seen by most users.

This PR proposes switching from `DeprecationWarning` to `FutureWarning`, the later should be visible by default. Python will print the first occurrence of matching warnings for each location.

Here's an example of a script using a deprecated function and its output:
```python
from urllib3.fields import format_header_param_rfc2231

def warn():
    print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.txt"))
    print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.pdf"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    warn()
    warn()
```

```
$ python format_header.py 
./format_header.py:4: FutureWarning: 'format_header_param_rfc2231' is insecure, deprecated and will be removed in urllib3 v3.0. This is not valid for multipart/form-data header parameters.
  print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.txt"))
filename="test.txt"
./format_header.py:5: FutureWarning: 'format_header_param_rfc2231' is insecure, deprecated and will be removed in urllib3 v3.0. This is not valid for multipart/form-data header parameters.
  print(format_header_param_rfc2231("filename", "test.pdf"))
filename="test.pdf"
filename="test.txt"
filename="test.pdf"
```


Related references:
https://sethmlarson.dev/deprecations-via-warnings-dont-work-for-python-libraries
https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3744
https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3731

issues.title: BaseHTTPResponse.readinto should accept any bytes-like object not just bytearray
issues.body:
### Subject

`BaseHTTPResponse.readinto` is implemented to provide compatibility with the io module 

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b90b2794cb3b462a1a190cecba2999c1d3c353e9/src/urllib3/response.py#L665-L673

However the implementation's typehinting is not compatible with what python docs say are valid inputs for the method.

https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.RawIOBase.readinto
> Read bytes into a pre-allocated, writable [bytes-like object](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-bytes-like-object) b

Where bytes-like objects can be any of: 
> object that supports the [Buffer Protocol](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/buffer.html#bufferobjects) and can export a C-[contiguous](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-contiguous) buffer. This includes all [bytes](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bytes), [bytearray](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bytearray), and [array.array](https://docs.python.org/3/library/array.html#array.array) objects, as well as many common [memoryview](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#memoryview) objects. ...

And detail most relevant here would be the read-write variant of bytes-like object https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-bytes-like-object
> Some operations need the binary data to be mutable. The documentation often refers to these as “read-write bytes-like objects”. Example mutable buffer objects include [bytearray](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bytearray) and a [memoryview](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#memoryview) of a [bytearray](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#bytearray).

### Environment

(not a runtime issue)

### Steps to Reproduce

```py
import io
import requests
from urllib3.response import HTTPResponse

with requests.get(url, stream=True) as response:
        data_stream = response.raw
        assert isinstance(data_stream, HTTPResponse)
        _ = io.BufferedReader(data_stream)
```

Run mypy on this snippet using typeshed for annotations for the io module

### Expected Behavior

mypy should pass this piece of code

### Actual Behavior

```
error: Argument 1 to "BufferedReader" has incompatible type "HTTPResponse"; expected "_BufferedReaderStream"  [arg-type]
note: Following member(s) of "HTTPResponse" have conflicts:
note:     Expected:
note:         def readinto(self, memoryview[int], /) -> int | None
note:     Got:
note:         def readinto(self, b: bytearray) -> int
```

---

I am also filing a issue with typeshed to improve the typing they provide for`_BufferedReaderStream`
https://github.com/python/typeshed/issues/15311
